prereqs: The RTL-to-GDSII flow end to end
Netlists as the shared currency of the flow
lesson:
# The PCB design flow

A printed circuit board flow takes a circuit drawn from purchased parts and turns it into copper, holes and assembly instructions. It starts where the chip flow ends: the silicon is already packaged, so the board tool never synthesizes logic. It captures connectivity, binds every part to a physical footprint, places and routes a few hundred to a few thousand packages on a few to a few dozen layers, checks the result and writes manufacturing data. A tool designer needs this map to see which engines exist, what each consumes and where errors leak between them.

## Stages of the board flow

The stages run in order. **Schematic capture** records components and nets. **Footprint assignment** binds each symbol to a land pattern. **Netlist transfer** moves connectivity and footprints into layout. **Placement** positions the packages, **routing** draws traces and vias on the stackup, **DRC** checks geometry and connectivity against the fabricator's rules, and **output generation** writes the fabrication data (Gerber or ODB++, drill files, stackup drawing) and the assembly data (BOM, centroid file, paste layers). Unlike the chip flow there is no synthesis, no standard-cell library and no foundry PDK. The parts are fixed packages, and the rules come from a board fabricator's process capability, usually expressed against IPC standards. A small board might be 2 layers and 50 parts; a server board might be 20 or more layers and several thousand parts.

## What crosses each boundary

Each handoff is a representation that preserves some facts and drops others. The **netlist** carries nets as lists of reference-designator and pin-number pairs, plus the footprint name of each part, and nothing geometric. The **board database** adds outline, stackup, placed footprints, traces, vias, pours and rules. The **fabrication outputs** are images and drill programs per layer; classic Gerber has no connectivity, so a separate IPC-D-356 netlist goes to bare-board test. The **assembly outputs** split by audience: the BOM tells purchasing what to buy, the centroid file tells the placement machine where each part goes and at what rotation, and the paste layers become the stencil. Two consumers, a bare-board fabricator and an assembler, see entirely different subsets of the design.

## Iteration and failure propagation

Board flows iterate just as chip flows do, and errors propagate downstream silently. A pinout error in a footprint passes every layout check, because the copper matches the netlist exactly; it fails only on the bench. A placement that crowds a BGA against a connector shows up later as unroutable channels, so the fix is upstream at placement. A stackup change from the fabricator after layout moves every controlled impedance, because impedance rises with dielectric height, so trace widths must be recomputed. The engineering rule is to fix a problem in the representation where it originates and push it forward: a mirrored connector is fixed in the library or schematic, then forward-annotated, never patched only in copper, because the next netlist update would undo the patch.

## Going deeper

Bogatin, "Signal and Power Integrity Simplified" (3rd ed., 2018), chapter 1, for why board interconnect is an engineering problem in its own right. The KiCad documentation, "Getting Started in KiCad", for a complete open-source walk through the flow.

label: Symbols, footprints and land patterns
lesson:
# Symbols, footprints and land patterns

Every board part exists in two views. The schematic symbol is logical: pins with names, numbers and electrical types. The footprint is physical: copper lands, solder mask and paste openings, silkscreen, a courtyard and often a 3D body. The land pattern is the copper part of the footprint that the terminations solder to. The binding between the two views is the pin number. Library data is the most reused data in board design, and its errors are invisible to every automated check, which is why tool designers treat libraries as verified, versioned artifacts.

## Two views of one part

A **symbol** carries pin names (VDD, SDA), pin numbers (1, 2, ...) and pin electrical types (input, output, bidirectional, passive, power input, power output). The types exist for the schematic ERC. A multi-unit symbol splits one package into units, so a dual op-amp appears as U1A and U1B on different sheets but maps to one footprint. A **footprint** carries lands numbered to match, plus layers for solder mask openings, solder paste apertures, silkscreen legend, an assembly outline and a **courtyard**, the keep-out envelope used by placement checks. A **land pattern**, in IPC terms, is the set of lands. Netlisting writes each connection as designator plus pin number, for example U3.14, and layout attaches it to land 14 of U3's footprint. Names are only for humans.

## Pin-to-pad errors and footprint layers

The classic library error is a pin-number mismatch. A transistor symbol numbered 1 = B, 2 = E, 3 = C, paired with a package whose vendor numbers 1 = B, 2 = C, 3 = E, yields a board with collector and emitter swapped. DRC passes, ERC passes, connectivity matches the netlist, and the board fails on the bench. The footprint's other layers each feed a different process. The **paste** layer becomes stencil apertures. The **mask** layer opens solder resist around lands, with a small expansion (often a few mils) so registration error between the copper and mask imaging steps never covers a land. The **courtyard** includes body, lands and an assembly margin, so two parts whose bodies clear can still collide in the courtyard check. Each layer answers a question for one downstream consumer.

## Land patterns from package tolerances

Land patterns are computed, not drawn. IPC-7351 derives land size from the package's dimensions and their tolerances, the fabrication tolerance and the placement tolerance, so that a worst-case part still forms a good **toe, heel and side fillet**. It defines three density levels, most, nominal and least material, which trade board density against joint robustness. Special features need care: a QFN's exposed thermal pad gets a paste window pane of several small openings covering roughly half its area, because one full opening floats the part and opens perimeter joints. A 3D body model lets the tool check clearance against the enclosure. Because one footprint is reused on every board that uses the part, organizations verify it once and freeze it in a shared library rather than letting designers draw parts per project.

## Going deeper

IPC-7351, "Generic Requirements for Surface Mount Design and Land Pattern Standard". The KiCad library conventions (KLC), for a published, checkable set of symbol and footprint rules.

B) The alphabetical order of the pin names

A) The pin's position on the schematic sheet

B) The pin name matching the net name

C) The alphabetical order of the pin names

D) The symbol pin number matching the footprint pad number
problems.a: The symbol pin number matching the footprint pad number

problems.q:
Why does each footprint carry a courtyard?

A) It is the paste stencil aperture

B) It is the keep-out envelope used to check component-to-component spacing during placement

C) It defines the copper pads

D) It sets the trace width to the pads
problems.a: It is the keep-out envelope used to check component-to-component spacing during placement
problems.e: The courtyard bounds the body, the pads and an assembly margin. Placement DRC checks courtyards for overlap so parts can be placed and reworked.

problems.q:
Which footprint layer becomes the solder stencil apertures?

A) The courtyard layer

B) The solder mask layer

C) The paste layer

D) The silkscreen layer
problems.a: The paste layer
problems.e: Paste openings define where solder paste is printed. Mask openings define where the board's mask is removed, which is a different layer for a different process.

problems.q:
A transistor symbol uses pins 1 = B, 2 = E, 3 = C, but the vendor's SOT-23 package is 1 = B, 2 = C, 3 = E. What happens?

A) ERC reports an output conflict

B) Gerber export fails

C) The board is built with collector and emitter swapped, and no layout check catches it

D) DRC reports a clearance violation
problems.a: The board is built with collector and emitter swapped, and no layout check catches it
problems.e: Copper matches the netlist exactly, so every check passes. The error lives in the pin-to-pad map, which is why library review is a separate discipline.

problems.q:
IPC-7351 defines three density levels for land patterns. What distinguishes them?

A) The number of copper layers in the board

B) The copper weight of the pads

C) The size of the toe, heel and side solder fillets: most, nominal and least material

D) Round pads versus square pads only
problems.a: The size of the toe, heel and side solder fillets: most, nominal and least material
problems.e: The levels trade density against solder-joint robustness. Dense consumer boards use smaller lands; rugged designs use larger fillets.

problems.q:
A QFN's exposed thermal pad is drawn with one full-size paste opening. Which assembly defect is likely?

A) Tombstoning of the QFN

B) No solder at all on the thermal pad

C) Mask-to-copper registration error

D) Excess solder that floats the part, causing voids or opens on the perimeter pins
problems.a: Excess solder that floats the part, causing voids or opens on the perimeter pins
problems.e: Large paste deposits lift the package. Footprints split the thermal paste into a window pane of smaller openings covering roughly half the area or a bit more.

problems.q:
A footprint carries a 3D body model. What can the tool check with it?

A) Netlist connectivity

B) The thermal-relief spoke width

C) Mechanical clearance against the enclosure and neighboring parts

D) Controlled impedance of the attached traces
problems.a: Mechanical clearance against the enclosure and neighboring parts
problems.e: 3D models feed collision checks with the mechanical CAD model of the enclosure. They do not affect the electrical checks.

label: Bills of materials
lesson:
# Bills of materials

The bill of materials (BOM) lists what must be bought and placed to build one board: one line per manufacturer part number, with its quantity, reference designators and approved sources. It is generated from the schematic, consumed by purchasing and the assembler, and must agree with the layout's footprints and the centroid file. A BOM tool groups placements, rolls up quantities for a build, and manages variants that leave some parts unpopulated. Each of these is a small, exact computation, and mistakes in it are expensive.

## One line per part number

A BOM line is keyed by the **manufacturer part number** (MPN), not by value. Placements R1 to R12 that all use one 10 kohm 0402 resistor MPN collapse into one line with quantity 12 and the designator list. The same value in a different package is a different MPN and a different line: a 100 nF 0402 capacitor and a 100 nF 0603 capacitor need different reels and feeders. Example: placements R1, R2 (10 kohm 0402), R3 (10 kohm 0603), C1, C2, C3 (100 nF 0402) and U1 (an LDO) make four lines. The grouping is a hash on the MPN field. Its correctness depends on the library, so a library with two MPN entries for one physical part silently splits a line and doubles the setup cost.

## Rolling up an order

Purchasing multiplies each line's per-board quantity by the build quantity and adds attrition, the parts lost to machine pick-up failures, splicing and setup. Small passives on reels are commonly ordered with a few percent extra, or with a fixed minimum per line. Example: a line with 12 placements per board, a build of 250 boards and 5% attrition needs $12 \cdot 250 \cdot 1.05 = 3150$ parts. When the product is fractional the order rounds up, since half a part cannot be bought. Real BOM tools then round further to the supplier's reel or cut-tape increments and check the approved alternate sources. The arithmetic is trivial; the failure mode is a stale BOM that no longer matches the schematic revision being built.

## Variants and DNP

One bare board often serves several products. A **variant** marks some lines **DNP** (do not populate): the land patterns remain in the copper, but the assembler does not place the part. A low-cost variant might drop an optional sensor and its decoupling, so its placement count is the sum of the populated lines only. Example: lines with quantities 12, 11 (DNP), 4 and 5 (DNP) give $12 + 4 = 16$ placements per board. Variants must flow consistently to every assembly output: the BOM, the centroid file and the assembly drawing must agree on which designators are fitted. A variant that is DNP in the BOM but present in the centroid file makes the machine try to pick a part that is not loaded, which stops the line.

## Going deeper

The IPC-2581 specification's BOM and component sections, for how a neutral format carries BOM, variants and placement in one file.

label: Netlist handoff and annotation
prereqs: Netlists as the shared currency of the flow
lesson:
# Netlist handoff and annotation

The netlist is the contract between schematic capture and layout. It lists each net as a set of pins, written as reference designator and pin number, and binds each designator to a footprint. Annotation assigns the designators; forward annotation pushes schematic changes into a layout in progress; back annotation returns layout-side changes such as gate swaps. Mathematically the netlist is a hypergraph. A tool designer must keep it consistent across two databases that are edited concurrently, which is a data-synchronization problem.

## Nets, labels and annotation

A schematic becomes a netlist by resolving connectivity. Wires join pins on one sheet. **Net labels** join wires by name, with scope: a local label connects only within its sheet, a global label everywhere, and power symbols such as GND or +3V3 act as global labels, so one misspelled power name silently creates a separate floating net. Hierarchical sheets connect through sheet pins, which lets one sheet be instantiated several times without its local nets shorting together. **Annotation** assigns unique reference designators (R12, U3). The result is a hypergraph: components are vertices and each net is a hyperedge on the pins it joins, the same structure chip tools use. A net with a single pin is suspicious, since it connects nothing.

## Forward and back annotation

Design does not stop when layout starts. **Forward annotation** pushes schematic edits (a changed value, an added capacitor, a reconnected pin) into the layout as an incremental update, keeping placed and routed parts. **Back annotation** returns layout decisions: swapping two equivalent NAND inputs or two gates of a quad package shortens routes, and the schematic must be updated so it still describes the board. Libraries declare which pins and gates are swappable; anything else changes the circuit. To survive renumbering, tools match components by a hidden unique identifier rather than by designator. If they matched by designator, renaming R7 to R12 would rip up the placed R7 and drop a new unplaced R12, or worse, attach R7's placement to a different part.

## Consistency checks across the boundary

The schematic and the board are two databases that must agree. After an import, a ratsnest line to an unrelated part usually means a symbol and footprint number their pins differently. After routing, a **connectivity check** extracts which lands the copper joins and compares those nets with the netlist, reporting opens (a net split in copper) and shorts (two nets merged), the board analogue of LVS. At fabrication, an **IPC-D-356** netlist goes with the Gerbers so the bare-board tester can probe every net for continuity and isolation before parts are mounted. When schematic and layout come from different tools, the netlist is exported in a format the layout tool imports, and the fragile part is mapping footprint names between the two libraries.

## Going deeper

The KiCad documentation on schematic hierarchy, labels and the update-PCB-from-schematic flow. Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 1, for the hypergraph view of netlists.

problems.e: Forward annotation pushes schematic edits to layout as an incremental update, so existing placement and routing survive.

lesson:
# Electrical rule checking of schematics

Electrical rule checking (ERC) runs on the schematic before layout. It reads each net's pins and their declared electrical types and flags combinations that cannot work: two outputs fighting, an input that nothing drives, a power input with no source, a net with a single pin. ERC is a set of cheap, exact predicates over the netlist hypergraph. It catches connectivity mistakes early, when they cost nothing to fix, but it knows only pin types, not the parts' datasheets.

## Pin types and the conflict matrix

Every symbol pin carries a type: input, output, bidirectional, tri-state, passive, open collector, power input, power output, or unconnected. ERC tools encode which types may share a net in a **pin conflict matrix**: output with output is an error (two drivers fight), output with input is fine, passive with anything is usually fine. The matrix is configuration, so a team can tighten or relax it. A net that touches only one pin is flagged too, since it connects nothing; a pin deliberately left open gets a no-connect marker so the check knows the intent. Power pins are special: KiCad, for example, reports a power input that no power output drives, which is why designs fed from a connector add a power flag symbol to declare the source.

## Evaluating the rules net by net

ERC is a pass over nets. For each net, count pins by type and evaluate each rule as a predicate on the counts. With the rules (a) exactly one pin, (b) two or more outputs or power outputs, (c) an input but no output, bidirectional, passive or power-output pin, and (d) a power input but no power output, consider three nets. N1 has an output and two inputs: no rule fires. N2 has two outputs and an input: rule (b) fires. N3 has two inputs and a bidirectional pin: rule (c) does not fire, since a bidirectional pin can drive. Count N2 once even if it broke two rules. The work is linear in the number of pins, so ERC runs interactively after every edit.

## What ERC cannot see

ERC reasons only about declared pin types, so it inherits every library mistake. A symbol that marks an output pin as passive hides a real conflict. It cannot see that a regulator's output capacitor is below the datasheet minimum, that an I2C bus lacks pull-ups (a passive pull-up and an open-drain pin are both legal), or that a 3.3 V output drives a 1.8 V input. Those are semantic checks that need part parameters and datasheet rules. Treating ERC warnings as noise is the common failure: a design with hundreds of waived warnings hides the one real error. Good flows keep the conflict matrix strict, annotate intentional exceptions explicitly, and add parameter-aware checks on top, which is where review agents can help.

lesson:
# The PCB tool landscape

Board design tools range from open-source suites to enterprise platforms. For a tool designer the useful questions are not which buttons they have, but what data model each exposes, how open its file formats and scripting are, how it represents constraints, and how designs move between tools. This lesson maps the main families: KiCad, LibrePCB and gEDA/Lepton in open source; Altium Designer, Cadence Allegro and OrCAD, Siemens Xpedition and PADS, Zuken, and Autodesk's EAGLE lineage commercially.

## Open-source tools

**KiCad** is the most widely used open-source suite: schematic and PCB editors, an interactive push-and-shove router, a 3D viewer and a Python scripting interface. Its schematics and boards are readable S-expression text files, which makes them diffable and parseable by external tools. **LibrePCB** is built around a versioned library in which every symbol, package and device is identified by a UUID, so libraries can be shared without name clashes. **gEDA** was an early open toolkit (a schematic editor, the netlister gnetlist and the pcb layout tool); **Lepton EDA** is a community fork of the gEDA schematic and netlisting tools, scripted in Guile Scheme, with netlist back ends written as small Scheme programs. **Freerouting** is an open-source autorouter that exchanges boards through Specctra DSN and SES files.

## Commercial families

**Altium Designer** is a unified schematic, layout and library environment, paired with Altium's cloud collaboration service. **Cadence** offers **OrCAD** (OrCAD Capture for schematics and mainstream layout) and **Allegro**, an enterprise layout platform with a central constraint manager. **Siemens** offers **Xpedition** for enterprise design and **PADS** for mainstream design, both from its Mentor Graphics acquisition. **Zuken** offers **CR-8000** and **eCADSTAR**. **EAGLE** was acquired by Autodesk from CadSoft, and Autodesk moved its electronics capability into the Fusion electronics workspace. Enterprise tools emphasize what large teams need: a shared constraint system, concurrent multi-user editing, library governance and packaging co-design, rather than drawing features.

## Data models and interoperability

For automation, a tool's data model matters more than its editor. Text formats with a scripting API (KiCad) let a team run custom checks across hundreds of designs; binary formats confine automation to the vendor's API. Moving a design between tools preserves connectivity and geometry best, because every tool has nets, footprints, traces and vias. **Constraints** translate worst, because each tool models net classes, matching groups and rule scopes differently, so they are usually rebuilt by hand. Neutral formats help at the edges: Specctra DSN hands a placed board to an external router, IPC-2581 and ODB++ carry a finished board to manufacturing, and the gEDA netlister's pluggable back ends show the seam pattern, one stable connectivity model with many small format writers.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Stackup build: thickness, layer count and symmetry

A stackup is the ordered list of copper layers and dielectrics that make up the board: cores, prepregs, copper weights and the finished thickness. It sets every impedance, the via aspect ratio, the layer count available to routing and the board's mechanical flatness. The layout tool stores it as a table that every SI calculation reads, and the fabricator turns it into a lamination recipe. Three computations recur: finished thickness, the number of cores and prepregs, and a symmetry check.

## Cores, prepreg and copper

A **core** is a cured glass-epoxy laminate with copper on both sides. **Prepreg** is glass cloth with partly cured resin that flows and cures in the lamination press, bonding cores and foils. Copper weight is quoted in ounces per square foot: 1 oz is about 1.37 mil (35 micrometres) thick. Finished thickness is the sum of the dielectrics plus the copper. Example: a 4-layer stack of 1 oz, 8 mil prepreg, 1 oz, 40 mil core, 1 oz, 8 mil prepreg, 1 oz has $56 + 4 \cdot 1.37 = 61.48$ mil, close to the common 62 mil board. Real fabricators adjust for resin flow into inner copper, plating on outer layers and solder mask, which is why the fabricator's stackup proposal, not the designer's estimate, is the reference.

## Layer count and construction

Most boards use an even number of copper layers, because cores carry copper in pairs. In a **foil build** of an $L$-layer board, the inner layers sit on $(L - 2)/2$ cores, and the two outer layers are copper foils pressed onto prepreg. The board has $L - 1$ dielectric layers, so $L - 1 - (L - 2)/2 = L/2$ of them are prepreg. An 8-layer foil build has 3 cores and 4 prepreg layers. Layer count is chosen from routing demand (how many signal layers BGA escape needs), the number of reference planes high-speed signals require, and power distribution. Each signal layer should sit next to a solid reference plane, which is why a typical 6-layer board has 4 signal layers or fewer.

## Symmetry and why boards warp

A stackup should be **symmetric** about its center: layer $k$ and layer $L + 1 - k$ with the same copper weight, and each dielectric matching its mirror. Copper and glass-epoxy expand at different rates, so an unbalanced stack bends during lamination cooling and again in every reflow, producing bow and twist that break BGA joints and jam assembly fixtures. A symmetry check compares mirrored pairs: in a 6-layer stack there are 3 copper pairs and 2 dielectric pairs, since the center dielectric mirrors onto itself. Copper distribution matters too: a solid plane mirrored by a sparse signal layer is unbalanced even with equal weights, so designers add copper thieving or balance planes. A stackup editor can run this check automatically on every edit.

## Going deeper

# Trace resistance from copper weight

A trace is a resistor of rectangular cross-section. Its resistance sets the DC voltage drop on power traces, the loss at low frequency, and the self-heating that limits current. Board tools compute it from the stackup's copper weight and the trace geometry, and a power-integrity tool sums it over thousands of shapes. The model is $R = \rho L / (w t)$ with the resistivity of copper, corrected for temperature.

## Resistance from geometry

For a uniform conductor, $R = \rho L / A$ with $A = w t$. Copper's resistivity is about $1.72 \times 10^{-8}\ \Omega\cdot$m at 20 C. The thickness $t$ comes from the copper weight: 1 oz is about 35 micrometres, 2 oz about 70. Example: a trace 100 mm long and 0.25 mm wide in 1 oz copper has $A = 0.25 \times 10^{-3} \cdot 35 \times 10^{-6} = 8.75 \times 10^{-9}$ square metres, so $R = 1.72 \times 10^{-8} \cdot 0.1 / 8.75 \times 10^{-9} \approx 0.197\ \Omega$, about 197 milliohms. A handy form is sheet resistance: 1 oz copper is about 0.5 milliohm per square, so the trace above, $100/0.25 = 400$ squares long, has about 200 milliohms. Unit discipline is the main source of error: convert every length to metres first.

## Voltage drop on power traces

Ohm's law turns resistance into the drop a load sees. A 0.2 ohm trace carrying 2 A drops 0.4 V, which would be fatal for a 1.0 V core rail with a 3% tolerance (30 mV). That is why power is distributed on planes or wide pours, and why regulators use **remote sense**, measuring the voltage at the load and adjusting their output to cancel the drop. On a plane, current spreads, and the resistance between a regulator and a BGA depends on the plane's geometry and the vias that feed it; a DC power-integrity tool solves a resistive mesh, a sparse linear system of nodal equations, to find the drop at every pin. A single trace is the one-dimensional special case.

## Temperature and frequency effects

Copper's resistance rises with temperature by about 0.393% per C: $R_T = R_{20}(1 + 0.00393 (T - 20))$. A trace at 85 C has about 26% more resistance than at 20 C, so a drop budget must be checked hot, and a trace that heats itself raises its own resistance, a feedback that current-capacity rules account for. At high frequency the **skin effect** confines current to a layer near the surface, about 2 micrometres thick at 1 GHz in copper, so a 35 micrometre trace uses only a fraction of its cross-section and its AC resistance grows roughly with the square root of frequency. Surface roughness adds more loss. DC resistance is therefore a lower bound for signal loss, accurate only for power and slow signals.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Trace current capacity rules of thumb

How wide must a trace be to carry a given current? The trace heats from $I^2 R$ loss and cools through the laminate and the air, so the answer is a temperature-rise limit, not a hard current limit. Board tools still use empirical rules, the oldest being the IPC-2221 chart fit, which a constraint system turns into minimum widths per net class. Knowing the rule, its inversion and its limits lets a tool designer implement width checks honestly.

## The IPC-2221 chart fit

IPC-2221 gives a curve fit to old test data: $I = k\, \Delta T^{0.44} A^{0.725}$, with $I$ in amperes, the temperature rise $\Delta T$ in C, the cross-section $A$ in square mils, $k = 0.048$ for outer layers and $k = 0.024$ for inner layers. Example: a 10 mil outer trace in 1 oz copper has $A = 10 \cdot 1.37 = 13.7$ square mils. For a 10 C rise, $I = 0.048 \cdot 10^{0.44} \cdot 13.7^{0.725} \approx 0.048 \cdot 2.754 \cdot 6.67 \approx 0.88$ A. Current grows slower than linearly with area (exponent 0.725), because a wider trace has proportionally less surface per unit cross-section through which to shed heat. Doubling the allowed rise raises the current only by $2^{0.44} \approx 1.36$.

## Inverting the rule for width

Constraint checks need the inverse: the minimum width for a current. Solve for area, $A = (I / (k\, \Delta T^{0.44}))^{1/0.725}$, then divide by thickness. Example: 2 A with a 10 C rise on an outer 1 oz layer gives $A = (2 / (0.048 \cdot 2.754))^{1.379} \approx 15.13^{1.379} \approx 42.4$ square mils, so $w = 42.4 / 1.37 \approx 31$ mil. On an inner layer $k$ halves, and the area must grow by $2^{1/0.725} \approx 2.6$, to about 80 mil. Heavier copper helps directly: 2 oz halves the width for the same area. A width rule per net class, computed this way, is what the DRC enforces on power nets.

## Limits of the rule

The IPC-2221 curves come from limited tests decades ago, and the inner-layer constant is a conservative halving rather than a measurement. **IPC-2152** replaced the chart with newer data showing that board thickness, nearby copper planes and the laminate's thermal conductivity matter as much as the layer position; planes spread heat well, so internal traces next to planes often run cooler than the old rule predicts. Neither rule handles short neck-downs, many parallel hot traces, or vias, which have their own current limits. A tool that reports one number should say which rule produced it. For high-current designs the honest method is a thermal simulation, using the rule of thumb only to size the first draft.

## Going deeper

# Stackups and controlled impedance

A fast edge on a board trace travels as a wave on a transmission line made of the trace and its reference plane. Its characteristic impedance $Z_0 = \sqrt{L/C}$ per unit length is set by the trace width, the copper thickness, the dielectric height to the plane and the dielectric constant. Controlled impedance means choosing those numbers so every critical net has, say, 50 ohms single-ended, and having the fabricator build to that target. Board tools embed closed-form approximations and 2D field solvers for this; the closed forms show the trends.

## Microstrip impedance

A **microstrip** is a trace on an outer layer over a plane, with dielectric below and air above. IPC-2141 gives the approximation $Z_0 = \frac{87}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_r + 1.41}} \ln\frac{5.98 h}{0.8 w + t}$ for $h$ the height to the plane, $w$ the width and $t$ the copper thickness, all in one length unit, reasonable for $w/h$ between about 0.1 and 2. Example: $h = 5$ mil, $w = 8$ mil, $t = 1.4$ mil, $\varepsilon_r = 4.2$ gives $87/\sqrt{5.61} = 36.7$ and $\ln(29.9 / 7.8) = 1.344$, so $Z_0 \approx 49.4$ ohms. The formula is a fit, accurate to several percent; signoff uses a 2D field solver that also models solder mask, which lowers a microstrip's impedance by a few ohms.

## Stripline impedance

A **stripline** is a trace buried between two planes, fully surrounded by dielectric. For a trace centered between planes $b$ apart, IPC-2141 gives $Z_0 = \frac{60}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_r}} \ln\frac{1.9 b}{0.8 w + t}$. Example: $b = 16$ mil, $w = 5$ mil, $t = 0.7$ mil, $\varepsilon_r = 4.0$ gives $30 \cdot \ln(30.4 / 4.7) = 30 \cdot 1.867 \approx 56$ ohms. Two planes add capacitance, so a stripline needs a narrower trace than a microstrip for the same impedance, and its field is entirely in the dielectric, which slows it and removes the odd and even velocity difference that causes far-end crosstalk. Real stacks often place the trace off-center (asymmetric stripline) or route two signal layers between a pair of planes, which needs the field solver.

## Sensitivities and fabrication tolerance

The formulas encode the trends a designer must know: impedance **rises with height** (log of $h$ or $b$), **falls with width** and thickness (log of $0.8w + t$), and **falls with the dielectric constant** (as $1/\sqrt{\varepsilon_r}$ roughly). Because the dependence is logarithmic, a 1 mil error on a 4 mil dielectric moves impedance far more than on a 10 mil one. Fabricators quote controlled impedance with a tolerance, commonly 10%, and adjust trace width and prepreg choice within limits to hit it, which is why the drawing names target impedances and reference layers rather than freezing widths. A tool should store the target and recompute the width when the stackup changes, not store a width alone.

# Propagation delay and effective dielectric constant

A signal on a board trace moves at the speed of light divided by the square root of the effective dielectric constant the field sees. That gives a delay per inch for each layer, the number that converts lengths into time for every length-matching constraint and every timing budget at board level. Microstrip and stripline in the same laminate have different delays, so equal lengths are not equal times.

## Delay in a homogeneous dielectric

Light travels about 11.8 inches per ns in vacuum. In a medium with relative permittivity $\varepsilon_{eff}$, the speed is $c/\sqrt{\varepsilon_{eff}}$, so the delay per inch is $t_{pd} = \sqrt{\varepsilon_{eff}}/11.8$ ns. A stripline is fully embedded, so $\varepsilon_{eff} = \varepsilon_r$. Example: $\varepsilon_r = 4.0$ gives $2/11.8 = 0.1695$ ns, about 170 ps per inch, the familiar rule of roughly 6 inches per ns on FR-4. Delay grows only as the square root of the dielectric constant: going from 4.0 to 3.4 (a low-loss laminate) shortens delay by about 8%. The value to use is the dielectric constant at the signal's frequency, since laminate Dk falls slowly with frequency.

## Effective dielectric constant of microstrip

A microstrip's field is partly in the laminate and partly in the air above, so it sees an **effective** dielectric constant between 1 and $\varepsilon_r$. A common approximation for typical FR-4 geometries is $\varepsilon_{eff} \approx 0.475\,\varepsilon_r + 0.67$. Example: $\varepsilon_r = 4.2$ gives $\varepsilon_{eff} = 2.665$, so $t_{pd} = \sqrt{2.665}/11.8 \approx 138$ ps per inch, against 174 ps per inch for stripline in the same laminate. More exact forms depend on $w/h$; field solvers compute $\varepsilon_{eff}$ directly as the ratio of the line's capacitance with and without the dielectric. Solder mask over the trace raises $\varepsilon_{eff}$ slightly, and so does any coating applied after assembly.

## Delay of a mixed route

A routed net usually changes layers. Its delay is the sum over segments of length times that layer's delay, plus the vias. Example, in a laminate with $\varepsilon_r = 4.0$: 1.0 inch of microstrip at about 136 ps per inch and 3.0 inches of stripline at 169.5 ps per inch give $135.9 + 508.5 \approx 644$ ps. Two nets of equal total length but different layer mixes can differ by tens of ps, which exceeds many matching budgets. That is why board tools match **delay**, not raw length, once nets change layers: the constraint system stores a per-layer delay table derived from the stackup and converts each segment. A via adds its own delay, often modeled as an equivalent length, which tools let the designer specify.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Flex and rigid-flex boards

Flexible circuits put copper on thin polyimide film so the board can bend, either once at installation or repeatedly in service. Rigid-flex boards laminate flexible layers through rigid sections and leave them bare in between, replacing connectors and cables. The design rules change: materials, coverlay instead of mask, bend-radius limits, routing across bends and plane hatching. Board tools model flex regions as zones of the stackup with their own layer sets and rules.

## Flex materials and construction

The base dielectric of a flex circuit is **polyimide** film, which survives soldering temperatures and bends without cracking. Copper is often **rolled-annealed**, whose elongated grains resist fatigue better than electrodeposited copper, which matters for hinges that flex thousands of times. Instead of liquid solder mask, which cracks, flex uses a **coverlay**: polyimide film with adhesive, laminated over the circuit with openings at pads. In **rigid-flex**, the flexible layers continue through the rigid sections, where FR-4 layers are laminated onto them, and are left exposed in the bend region. The board tool therefore needs a stackup per region: the rigid stack, the flex stack, and the transitions where coverlay and rigid material end.

## Bend radius rules

Bending strains the outer copper in proportion to its distance from the neutral axis over the bend radius, so the minimum bend radius scales with the flex thickness. Fabricators publish rules of the form radius at least $k$ times thickness, with $k$ growing with the number of copper layers and much larger for **dynamic** flexing (repeated bending in service) than for **static** bends made once at installation. Example with a rule of 12 times thickness for two copper layers: a 0.2 mm two-layer flex needs at least 2.4 mm; if the same section must flex continuously under a 100 times rule, it needs 20 mm. IPC-2223 gives guidance; the fabricator's own numbers govern. A DRC can check bend lines drawn in the mechanical layer against these limits.

## Routing and features in flex regions

Traces should cross a bend **perpendicular** to the bend line and be staggered between layers, not stacked, because stacked traces act like an I-beam that stiffens the section and concentrates strain. Corners are rounded, traces get teardrops at pads, and **vias and pads stay out of bend areas**, since a rigid plated barrel is a stress riser. Planes in flex are often **cross-hatched** to keep the section flexible, which changes the impedance of traces referenced to them and must be modeled. **Stiffeners** (FR-4 or polyimide bonded locally) support connector and component areas so joints are not flexed. Rigid-flex costs more to fabricate, but it removes connectors and cables, which are a common source of field failures, and saves volume.

## Going deeper

IPC-2223, "Sectional Design Standard for Flexible/Rigid-Flexible Printed Boards". Fjelstad, "Flexible Circuit Technology" (4th ed., 2011).

lesson:
# Via types

A via is a plated hole that connects copper on different layers. Its type is defined by which layers it spans and how it is made: through vias span the whole board, blind vias start at an outer layer and stop inside, buried vias join only inner layers, and microvias are small laser-drilled blind structures spanning one dielectric. Via type drives cost, density, routing capacity and signal integrity. A board router models each type as a layer span with its own cost and rules.

## Through, blind, buried and micro

A **through via** is mechanically drilled through the finished laminated stack and plated in one step; it is the cheapest via and connects to any layer it passes. A **blind via** is visible on one surface and ends at an inner layer. A **buried via** joins inner layers only; its sub-stack is drilled and plated before the outer layers are laminated over it, so every distinct buried span is an extra process sequence. A **microvia** is laser-drilled through a single thin dielectric, with an aspect ratio of at most 1:1 in current IPC usage. In a router, a via is an edge between layer graphs, annotated with the span it occupies and a cost. A through via blocks every layer; a blind or buried via blocks only the layers it spans, which is its routing value.

## Pads, antipads and fanout structures

Each via has a **pad** on the layers it connects and an **antipad**, a clearance opening, on the planes it passes without connecting. The antipad size sets the via's capacitance to the planes and hence its impedance. On fine-pitch BGAs, a via cannot fit between pads; **via-in-pad** places it in the land, and the hole must be filled and plated over so solder does not wick into it during reflow. Microvias can be **stacked**, each on a copper-filled one below, which is compact but concentrates thermal-cycling stress at the interfaces, or **staggered**, offset from each other, which uses more area and is generally more robust. These choices change the DRC rule set the router must obey per via type.

## Via stubs and resonance

A through via that carries a signal from L1 to L3 of a 12-layer board leaves the barrel below L3 unused: an open-ended **stub**. A stub resonates when it is a quarter wavelength long, $f_0 = c / (4 L \sqrt{\varepsilon_r})$, where it notches the channel's transmission. Example: a 60 mil stub in $\varepsilon_r = 4.0$ gives $11.8 / (4 \cdot 0.06 \cdot 2) \approx 24.6$ GHz, while a 120 mil stub puts the notch near 12.3 GHz, inside the band of a 25 Gbaud NRZ link whose Nyquist frequency is 12.5 GHz. Fixes are to route on layers that use most of the barrel, to **backdrill** the stub from the far side with a controlled-depth drill, or to use blind vias. The stub length is a direct output of layer assignment, so a router that knows the channel's band can choose layers to keep stubs short.

## Going deeper

IPC-2226, "Sectional Design Standard for High Density Interconnect Printed Boards". Bogatin, "Signal and Power Integrity Simplified" (3rd ed., 2018), chapter on via discontinuities.

lesson:
# Via aspect ratios and drill limits

The aspect ratio of a plated hole is its depth divided by its drilled diameter. It limits how well plating solution reaches the middle of the barrel, so fabricators cap it, and the cap ties the board thickness to the smallest through via. Microvias have their own cap, near 1:1, which ties the build-up dielectric thickness to the laser drill size. These are simple divisions, but they set the density floor of the whole design.

## Through-hole aspect ratio

For a through via, aspect ratio is board thickness divided by drilled hole diameter, written $x$:1. Example: a 62 mil board with 10 mil drills has 6.2:1. Plating builds copper on the barrel wall by electrochemical deposition; in a deep, narrow hole the solution exchanges poorly and the current density falls in the middle, so the copper there thins. Thin barrel copper cracks under the expansion of the laminate in thermal cycling, one of the classic board reliability failures. That is why IPC performance classes specify minimum barrel plating thickness, and why fabricators publish a maximum aspect ratio for reliable plating. A drill-table check in DRC computes the ratio for every hole size against the stackup thickness.

## Minimum drill from a fab limit

Inverting the ratio gives the smallest allowed drill: $d_{min} = T / AR_{max}$, rounded up to the drill increment. Example: a fabricator that plates reliably to 10:1 and a 93 mil board give $d_{min} = 9.3$ mil, so 10 mil drills. Thicker boards, needed for high layer counts or connector press-fit, therefore force larger vias, larger pads and fewer routing channels between BGA balls. Designers respond by choosing a thinner board, by moving fanout to blind or microvias whose depth is much smaller than the board, or by paying for an advanced fabricator with a higher limit. Finished hole size is smaller than drill size by twice the plating thickness, so drawings must say which one a number means.

## Microvia aspect ratio

A microvia's depth is the thickness of the dielectric it spans, usually one build-up layer. Laser-drilled holes are cone-shaped and are plated or filled from one side, so the reliable aspect ratio is near 1:1 or lower; many fabricators cap it at 0.75:1 to 1:1. Example: a 4 mil laser drill and a 0.8:1 cap allow dielectrics up to 3.2 mil, so a 3 mil build-up qualifies and a 4 mil one does not. This couples stackup choice to via technology: the build-up dielectric thickness, which also sets the impedance of outer-layer traces, must satisfy the microvia rule. A stackup editor that knows the drill table can flag the conflict as soon as the dielectric is chosen.

## Going deeper

IPC-6012, "Qualification and Performance Specification for Rigid Printed Boards", on plating thickness by class. IPC-2226 on microvia structures.

lesson:
# HDI build-ups and microvia stacking

High-density interconnect (HDI) boards add thin build-up layers to a conventional core, connected by laser-drilled microvias, so fine-pitch BGAs can escape without through vias. They are described by the notation $i + N + i$: an $N$-layer core with $i$ sequential build-up layers on each side. The notation fixes the layer count, the number of lamination and drilling cycles, and how many via structures a connection stacks, which together drive cost and reliability.

## The i plus N plus i notation

In $i + N + i$, the core is a conventional $N$-layer board, often with buried through-core vias, and $i$ build-up layers are added on each side. The total is $2i + N$ layers. A 1+6+1 board has 8 layers; a 2+4+2 board also has 8, but with two sequential build-ups per side. The top build-up layers are L1 to $Li$, the core spans $L(i+1)$ to $L(i+N)$, and the bottom build-up layers follow. The notation tells a router which layer spans are available: microvias between adjacent build-up layers and from the outer build-up to the core surface, buried vias through the core, and possibly through vias. "Any-layer" HDI makes every layer a build-up layer with microvias between any adjacent pair.

## Sequential lamination and drilling

Each build-up layer is added in its own cycle: laminate a dielectric and copper foil onto both sides, laser-drill microvias, plate, image and etch. With the core laminated once, an $i + N + i$ board needs $1 + i$ lamination cycles: a 2+4+2 board needs 3. Drilling follows the same structure: one mechanical drill of the core for buried vias, one laser-drill step per build-up layer per side, and one final mechanical drill for through holes, $2i + 2$ operations in all for a board that uses every kind. Each cycle adds press time, registration error between layers, yield loss and cost, which is why HDI price rises steeply with $i$ and why designers try a 1+N+1 build before a 2+N+2.

## Stacked connections and reliability

A connection from L1 into the core uses one microvia per build-up layer, stacked or staggered, and then the buried via. Example on a 2+6+2 board: L1 to L5 uses microvias L1 to L2 and L2 to L3 (the core's top), then the buried via from L3 through the core, which also connects L4 to L8, so 3 via structures. A connection from L1 to L10 uses 2 microvias, the buried via and 2 more microvias, 5 structures. Every interface between stacked microvias, and between a microvia and the buried via's cap, is a place where thermal-cycling stress concentrates; stacked microvias over buried vias have shown latent failures, so many designs stagger them. A layer-assignment engine can count structures per connection and penalize deep stacks as a reliability cost, not just a fabrication cost.

## Going deeper

IPC-2226, "Sectional Design Standard for High Density Interconnect Printed Boards". Holden, "The HDI Handbook" (2009).

lesson:
# Board placement and ratsnest length

Board placement positions a few hundred to a few thousand heterogeneous packages under mechanical, thermal, electrical and assembly constraints. Unlike chip placement, it is mostly interactive, guided by grouping from the schematic and by a live ratsnest: each net drawn as a minimum spanning tree over its pins. Total ratsnest length is the board placer's wirelength proxy. Knowing what it measures, how it is computed and what it misses is the core of placement quality.

## What drives board placement

Placement starts with **fixed** parts: connectors, mounting holes, switches, displays and anything else the enclosure dictates. Then come the parts that set the board's critical structure: the processor or FPGA, memory placed to keep its bus short, the power stages near the inputs they feed, and the clock sources. **Decoupling capacitors** go as close as possible to the power pins they serve, because their high-frequency benefit is limited by the loop inductance of the connection. Cross-probing from the schematic gathers each functional block so its local nets stay short. Courtyard checks run continuously, since courtyards include lands and an assembly margin. The placer is the designer, with the tool supplying constraints, metrics and checks.

## Ratsnest as a minimum spanning tree

The ratsnest shows unrouted connectivity. Each net with pins $p_1, \dots, p_k$ is drawn as a **minimum spanning tree** over the pins, usually with Manhattan or Euclidean distance, recomputed as parts move. Prim's algorithm on the complete graph of $k$ pins takes $O(k^2)$, which is fine for typical board nets. Example with Manhattan distance: pins listed as (0, 0), (10, 8), (10, 0) and (2, 9) give tree edges of 10, 8 and 9 for a length of 27, while chaining the pins in listed order gives $18 + 8 + 17 = 43$ and a star from the first pin gives $18 + 10 + 11 = 39$. The bounding-box half-perimeter, 10 plus 9 = 19, only lower-bounds the routed length. Summed over nets, ratsnest length is a quick, incremental placement score.

## What the ratsnest misses

Total ratsnest length weights every net equally and ignores everything but distance. A placement that saves 15% of total length but moves a DDR memory farther from its controller is worse, because those nets carry tight timing and SI limits. It ignores **noise coupling**: a switching regulator's inductor beside an analog input. It ignores **thermal** interaction: two hot parts side by side raise each other's junction temperature through shared copper. It ignores **assembly**: on a board reflowed twice, heavy parts on the bottom fall off in the second pass. A useful automatic placer must therefore weight nets, carry keep-out and proximity rules, and score thermal and assembly constraints, which is why board placement remains largely interactive.

label: Board autorouters versus chip routers
lesson:
# Board autorouters versus chip routers

Board and chip routers share algorithms (maze search, rip-up and reroute, negotiated congestion) but face different problems. A chip router handles millions of nets on a uniform track grid with preferred directions per layer. A board router handles thousands of nets with irregular pads, large obstacles, few layers, any-angle geometry, and electrical constraints such as differential pairs and length matching. That is why board routing is often interactive, with autorouting filling in the remainder.

## Shape-based routing on few layers

Board routers are mostly **shape-based** (gridless): they route against the exact polygons of pads, keep-outs and existing copper, with 45-degree or any-angle segments, rather than on a uniform grid of tracks. With 2 to a few dozen layers and big blockages such as BGAs and connectors, a strict horizontal-vertical layer split wastes too much capacity, so each layer routes in any direction. Routing starts with **fanout and escape**: bringing every BGA ball out to a via and a channel, which largely determines the layer count. The dominant interactive tool is the **push-and-shove** router, which moves existing traces and vias aside within clearance rules as the designer draws, keeping the board DRC-clean at every step.

## Shared algorithms

The algorithms carry over. A **maze router** expands a wavefront over a multilayer graph where vias are layer-change edges with an explicit cost, so it prefers fewer vias at equal length. Batch board autorouters iterate **rip-up and reroute** with costs that rise in contested regions, the same negotiation idea as chip global routing, over many passes until conflicts vanish or progress stalls. Power and ground mostly use planes, so the router only fans pins out to them. **Topological** routers first decide which side of each obstacle a wire passes (its homotopy class) and then compute geometry, spreading and smoothing wires afterwards. Boards reach external routers through interchange files such as Specctra DSN, which carries the outline, components, nets, rules and fixed wiring.

## Completion is not correctness

An autorouter's headline metric is completion: every net connected with clearance rules met. That says nothing about impedance (width and reference plane), length matching, return paths over plane splits, crosstalk between parallel runs, or via stubs. A differential pair routed as two independent nets takes different paths, losing coupling and adding skew. So designers route critical nets by hand first and **lock** them, define **net classes** with width, clearance, via and pair-gap rules, and then autoroute the rest. An AI or algorithmic router that is judged on completion alone will learn to trade the unmeasured constraints for completion. The fix is to measure them: post-route SI checks, length reports and constraint DRC become part of the router's acceptance test.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# BGA fanout and escape routing

A ball grid array puts hundreds or thousands of connections under one package. Escape routing brings each ball out from under the package to a routing channel, through traces between balls and vias down to other layers. How many traces fit between balls, how many rows each layer can escape, and how many balls sit in the outer rows together decide the board's layer count. These are geometric counts a tool designer can compute before any routing.

## Traces between adjacent balls

Between two adjacent lands of pitch $p$ and land diameter $d$, the gap is $p - d$. Fitting $N$ traces of width $w$ with clearance $s$ to the lands and to each other needs $N w + (N + 1) s \le p - d$, so $N = \lfloor (p - d - s)/(w + s) \rfloor$. Example: a 1.0 mm pitch with 0.5 mm lands and 0.1 mm trace and space gives $(0.5 - 0.1)/0.2 = 2$ traces. At 0.8 mm pitch with 0.4 mm lands and the same rules, $(0.4 - 0.1)/0.2 = 1.5$, so one trace. Finer pitch quickly drops $N$ to zero, at which point traces cannot pass between balls on the surface and the design needs via-in-pad, microvias or finer trace and space, all of which cost money.

## Rows escaped per layer

Under a simple model, the outer row escapes directly outward, and each trace that fits between balls lets one more row escape on the same layer, so each signal layer escapes $N + 1$ rows, from the outside in. Inner rows reach other layers through vias placed between balls (dog-bone fanout) or in the lands. A full $n \times n$ array has $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ concentric rows. Example: a 20 by 20 array has 10 rows; with one trace between balls, each layer escapes 2, so 5 signal layers are needed, before counting the power and ground balls, which go straight to planes and do not need escape. Real escape planning removes those balls first and often does better than the model by routing diagonal channels.

## Counting balls in the outer rows

How many signals each layer carries follows from counting balls in rings. The outer $k$ rows of a full $n \times n$ array contain $n^2 - (n - 2k)^2$ balls. Example: a 20 by 20 array's outer 2 rows hold $400 - 256 = 144$ balls, and the next 2 rows hold $256 - 144 = 112$. Outer rings hold the most balls, so the top layer does the most work, and each deeper layer carries fewer signals. This is why chip and package designers place high-speed signals on outer rows, which escape on the top layers with short via stubs, and put power and ground in the center, where they reach planes through short vias. Ball-map planning that knows the board's escape capacity is a classic package and board co-design problem.

## Going deeper

Holden, "The HDI Handbook" (2009), chapters on BGA escape. Xilinx and Intel FPGA PCB design guides, chapters on BGA breakout, for vendor-specific patterns.

prereqs: Transmission lines and the telegrapher's equations
lesson:
# Odd and even modes of coupled lines

Two traces routed side by side over a plane are coupled: each has mutual capacitance and mutual inductance to the other. Any pair of signals on them can be split into two modes, the odd mode (opposite voltages) and the even mode (equal voltages), each with its own impedance and velocity. Differential signaling lives in the odd mode, common-mode noise in the even mode. Field solvers in board tools report both, and every differential-pair rule is a statement about them.

## Two modes of a coupled pair

Drive line 1 with $V_1$ and line 2 with $V_2$. Write them as a differential part $V_1 - V_2$ and a common part $(V_1 + V_2)/2$; the **odd mode** carries the first (the lines at $+V$ and $-V$) and the **even mode** the second (both at $+V$). For a symmetric pair the modes are independent waves. In the odd mode the neighbor is at the opposite voltage, so the mutual capacitance $C_m$ charges through twice the voltage and adds to each line's capacitance, while the opposite currents make the mutual inductance $L_m$ subtract: $L_{odd} = L - L_m$, $C_{odd} = C + C_m$. In the even mode the reverse holds. Hence $Z_{odd} = \sqrt{(L - L_m)/(C + C_m)}$ falls below the uncoupled $Z_0$ and $Z_{even}$ rises above it as coupling tightens.

## Differential and common-mode impedance

A differential receiver sees the two lines in series, line to line, so the **differential impedance** is $Z_{diff} = 2 Z_{odd}$. A common-mode signal drives both lines in parallel against the reference, so the **common-mode impedance** is $Z_{cm} = Z_{even}/2$. Example: $Z_{odd} = 48$ ohms and $Z_{even} = 58$ ohms give $Z_{diff} = 96$ ohms and $Z_{cm} = 29$ ohms. A single 100 ohm resistor across the pair terminates only the odd mode; common-mode current flows through both lines in the same direction and never crosses that resistor. To terminate both modes, a T network puts $Z_{odd}$ from each line to a center node and $(Z_{even} - Z_{odd})/2$ from the node to ground: in the odd mode the node is a virtual ground, and in the even mode each line sees $Z_{even}$.

## Velocities, crosstalk and reference planes

In **microstrip** the odd mode puts more of its field in the air between and above the traces, so it sees a lower effective dielectric constant and travels faster than the even mode. That velocity difference is what produces far-end crosstalk: the capacitive and inductive coupling terms arrive at different times instead of cancelling. In **stripline** in a uniform dielectric both modes travel at one speed, and far-end crosstalk nearly vanishes. Board pairs are edge-coupled over a plane, and most of each trace's field still ends on the plane, which sets the impedances and returns common-mode current. A pair that crosses a split in its reference plane loses that symmetry, and part of its differential signal converts into common mode, which radiates and closes the eye.

## Going deeper

Hall and Heck, "Advanced Signal Integrity for High-Speed Digital Designs" (2009), chapter 3, on coupled transmission lines. Pozar, "Microwave Engineering" (4th ed., 2011), section on coupled lines.

label: Differential pairs
prereqs: Odd and even modes of coupled lines
lesson:
# Differential pairs

A differential pair carries one signal as the voltage difference between two traces. The receiver rejects noise that appears equally on both, the return current largely flows in the partner trace, and the fields of the two traces partly cancel, so pairs radiate less. Board interfaces specify a differential impedance, typically 85, 90 or 100 ohms, and the layout tool must translate it into trace width and gap. That translation goes through the odd and even mode impedances, and a TDR measurement goes back through them.

## From odd mode to differential impedance

A pair's differential impedance is twice its odd-mode impedance, $Z_{diff} = 2 Z_{odd}$, so a 100 ohm interface needs each trace to present 50 ohms in the odd mode. That is not the same as 50 ohms single-ended. When traces are tightly coupled, $Z_{odd}$ is well below the uncoupled $Z_0$, so each trace must be made narrower than a 50 ohm single-ended trace to bring $Z_{odd}$ back up to 50. A field solver sweeps width and gap to hit the target; the board tool stores the pair rule (width, gap, target) in a net class. Example: a solver reports $Z_{odd} = 46.1$ ohms for a candidate geometry, giving $Z_{diff} = 92.2$ ohms, close to a 90 ohm target and short of a 100 ohm one.

## Common-mode impedance

The common-mode impedance, $Z_{cm} = Z_{even}/2$, is what common-mode noise and the common-mode part of a signal see. It matters because receivers and connectors often specify a common-mode range or termination, and because unterminated common mode rings and radiates. For a loosely coupled pair, $Z_{even} \approx Z_{odd} \approx Z_0$, so $Z_{cm} \approx Z_0/2$ and $Z_{diff} \approx 2 Z_0$. Example: a pair with $Z_{odd} = 41.8$ and $Z_{even} = 44.8$ ohms is loosely coupled; $Z_{cm} = 22.4$ ohms. Tighter coupling raises $Z_{cm}$ and lowers $Z_{odd}$, separating the two numbers. A complete pair specification therefore names both, or names $Z_{diff}$ together with a geometry from which the solver derives $Z_{cm}$.

## Coupling from measured impedances

A TDR in differential mode measures $Z_{diff}$, and in common mode measures $Z_{cm}$. From them, $Z_{odd} = Z_{diff}/2$ and $Z_{even} = 2 Z_{cm}$, and the coupling coefficient $k = (Z_{even} - Z_{odd})/(Z_{even} + Z_{odd})$ summarizes how tightly the traces interact. Example: $Z_{diff} = 100$ and $Z_{cm} = 30$ ohms give $Z_{odd} = 50$, $Z_{even} = 60$ and $k = 10/110 \approx 0.091$. Small $k$ (wide gap) makes the impedance insensitive to gap variation and lets each trace be designed near 50 ohms single-ended, at the cost of area; large $k$ saves area and improves noise immunity between the pair's own traces, but etch variation in the gap moves the impedance more. The choice is a parameter a constraint system exposes, not a law.

## Going deeper

Bogatin, "Signal and Power Integrity Simplified" (3rd ed., 2018), chapter 11, on differential pairs.

prereqs: Propagation delay and effective dielectric constant
lesson:
# Length matching from a skew budget

Signals that must arrive together, the two traces of a differential pair or the data lines of a memory byte lane and their strobe, are given a skew budget in picoseconds. The layout tool turns that budget into a length tolerance using the layer's delay per inch, then tunes short traces with serpentines until every member of the group is inside the window. Matching is a timing constraint expressed in geometry, and the conversion is where errors creep in.

## Skew from a length mismatch

Skew is the arrival-time difference. For two traces on the same layer, skew equals the length difference times the delay per inch: $\Delta t = \Delta L \cdot t_{pd}$. Example: a 50 mil mismatch on a layer with 170 ps per inch is $0.05 \cdot 170 = 8.5$ ps. Within a differential pair, **intra-pair skew** turns part of the differential signal into common mode during the skewed interval, which shrinks the eye and raises emission; for multi-gigabit links the budget is a small fraction of the unit interval. Mismatch accumulates at every bend and pin: the inner trace of a turn is shorter than the outer, so routers compensate near the mismatch rather than at one end, keeping the two halves aligned along the whole route.

## Length tolerance from a budget

Inverting gives the tolerance: $\Delta L_{max} = \Delta t_{max} / t_{pd}$. Example: a 5 ps budget on stripline with $\varepsilon_r = 3.9$ has $t_{pd} = 1000\sqrt{3.9}/11.8 \approx 167.4$ ps per inch, so $\Delta L_{max} = 5/167.4 \approx 0.0299$ in, which rounds down to 29 mil; rounding up would exceed the budget. The budget itself comes from a timing analysis of the interface: setup and hold windows at the receiver minus driver uncertainty, jitter and other terms, so the length tolerance is a downstream product of a timing budget. When nets change layers the conversion must be per segment, which is why tools match delay rather than length.

## Matching a group to a strobe

In a memory byte lane every DQ must arrive within a window around its strobe, say $\pm 5$ ps. The tool computes each member's delay, compares it with the strobe's, and flags those outside the window. Example: a 2000 mil strobe at 160 ps per inch and a 5 ps window allow $\pm 31.25$ mil, so a 2040 mil DQ is outside the window: either it is shortened, or the strobe and the other members are lengthened toward it. Tuning adds **serpentines** (accordion meanders) to the short members. Meanders couple to themselves: parallel segments too close together let the signal shortcut through crosstalk, so the real delay added is less than the added length. Rules set a minimum gap between meander segments, often a few trace widths, and SI simulation confirms the result.

## Going deeper

JEDEC DDR4 and DDR5 design guides from memory vendors, for byte-lane matching rules. Bogatin, "Signal and Power Integrity Simplified" (3rd ed., 2018), on skew and mode conversion.

label: Reflections at board impedance discontinuities
lesson:
# Reflections at board impedance discontinuities

When a wave on a board trace meets a change of impedance, at a load, a via, a connector or a width change, part of it reflects. The reflection coefficient $\Gamma = (Z_L - Z_0)/(Z_L + Z_0)$ gives the fraction, and lattice bookkeeping of launched, reflected and transmitted waves predicts overshoot, ringing and settling. Board SI tools automate this with transmission-line simulation, but every termination decision rests on these three relations.

## The reflection coefficient

A wave of amplitude $V_i$ on a line of impedance $Z_0$ meets a load $Z_L$. Continuity of voltage and current at the junction gives a reflected wave $V_r = \Gamma V_i$ with $\Gamma = (Z_L - Z_0)/(Z_L + Z_0)$. Example: a 50 ohm trace into a 75 ohm load gives $\Gamma = 25/125 = 0.2$, a same-sign reflection; into 25 ohms, $\Gamma = -25/75 \approx -0.333$, an inverted one. An open end ($Z_L \to \infty$) gives $\Gamma = 1$, a short gives -1, and a matched load gives 0. CMOS inputs are nearly open, so an unterminated line reflects almost everything, and the reflection travels back to the source, where it reflects again with the source's own coefficient.

## Launch voltage and the first arrival

A driver with step $V_s$ and output resistance $R_s$ launches into a line as a voltage divider: $V_1 = V_s Z_0/(R_s + Z_0)$, because the line looks like $Z_0$ until any reflection returns. At the far end the voltage is the incident plus the reflected wave, $V_1(1 + \Gamma_L)$. Example: a 3.3 V driver with 20 ohms into a 50 ohm line launches $3.3 \cdot 50/70 = 2.357$ V; at a 1000 ohm load, $\Gamma_L = 0.905$, so the load jumps to about 4.49 V, an overshoot of 1.19 V above the rail. The reflection then returns to the source, where $\Gamma_S = (R_s - Z_0)/(R_s + Z_0) = -0.43$ inverts it, and the waveform rings down. A lattice diagram tracks these bounces until the net settles.

## Terminations and discontinuities

Terminations remove one of the two reflections. **Series** termination adds $R_t = Z_0 - R_s$ at the driver: the launched wave is half the swing, it doubles at the open receiver to the full swing, and the returning reflection is absorbed at the matched source. It suits point-to-point nets and costs no DC power. **Parallel** termination puts $Z_0$ at the far end, removing the load reflection but drawing DC current. Mid-line discontinuities, such as a connector, a via or a neck-down, both reflect and transmit: the transmitted fraction is $1 + \Gamma = 2 Z_2/(Z_1 + Z_2)$. A short discontinuity, electrically small compared with the rise time, acts as a lumped capacitance or inductance instead, which is why vias and pads matter more as edges get faster.

## Going deeper

Johnson and Graham, "High-Speed Digital Design" (1993), chapter 6, on terminations. Bogatin, "Signal and Power Integrity Simplified" (3rd ed., 2018), chapter 8.

lesson:
# IBIS models

IBIS (I/O Buffer Information Specification) is the standard behavioral model of a chip's I/O buffers for board-level signal integrity. Instead of a transistor netlist, the vendor publishes tables: current versus voltage for the pull-up, pull-down and clamp structures, voltage versus time for switching, die capacitance and package parasitics, each at typical, minimum and maximum corners. Board simulators combine IBIS buffers with transmission-line models of the routed nets. The format is a clean seam between the silicon vendor's IP and the board designer's analysis.

## What an IBIS model contains

An IBIS file is plain text organized by component and pin. For each buffer model it gives **V-I tables**: [Pullup] and [Pulldown] for the output stage, and [POWER Clamp] and [GND Clamp] for the protection diodes that conduct when the pin is driven above the supply or below ground. **V-t tables** ([Rising Waveform], [Falling Waveform]) give the output's switching behavior into specified test loads, and [Ramp] gives edge rates. **C_comp** is the die capacitance at the pad. The [Package] section gives lumped R_pkg, L_pkg and C_pkg, and per-pin values or package models can refine it. Every table has **typ, min and max** columns for process, voltage and temperature corners. Because it describes only pin behavior, it hides the transistor design and simulates far faster than SPICE.

## Reading drive strength from a V-I table

Near 0 V the [Pulldown] curve is nearly linear, and its slope gives the output resistance the line sees: $R = \Delta V / \Delta I$. Example: 0.2 V at 8 mA and 0.4 V at 16 mA give $0.2\ \text{V}/8\ \text{mA} = 25$ ohms. Farther out the transistor saturates, and the ratio of voltage to current at a saturated point (1.5 V at 30 mA, say, 50 ohms) is a large-signal number, not the small-signal resistance that sets the source reflection coefficient $\Gamma_S = (R - Z_0)/(R + Z_0)$. With $R = 25$ ohms on a 50 ohm line, $\Gamma_S = -1/3$, and a series terminator of about 25 ohms would match the source. The simulator uses the full nonlinear curve; the slope is what a designer uses to choose termination.

## Corners, power and the limits of IBIS

A simulation at the typ corner alone is incomplete: the fast-strong corner (max column) gives the worst overshoot, ringing and crosstalk, and the slow-weak corner (min) the worst timing, so SI runs bracket both. Classic IBIS assumes an ideal supply; when many outputs switch at once, the local rail sags and the buffers slow, so power-aware features tie output behavior to supply current for simultaneous switching noise analysis. Lumped package R, L and C are too coarse when package traces are electrically long or pins couple, and are replaced by per-pin or S-parameter package models. Finally, tables cannot express adaptive equalization in multi-gigabit SerDes, which is why IBIS-AMI adds executable algorithmic models.

## Going deeper

The IBIS specification, maintained by the IBIS Open Forum. Hall and Heck, "Advanced Signal Integrity for High-Speed Digital Designs" (2009), chapter on I/O buffer modeling.

label: Touchstone files and channel S-parameters
lesson:
# Touchstone files and channel S-parameters

Passive board structures at high frequency, such as traces, vias, connectors and packages, are described by scattering parameters measured or simulated over frequency. The Touchstone file format (.sNp) is the common container: one frequency per row, $N^2$ complex S-parameters for an $N$-port network. Channel simulators cascade these blocks between transmitter and receiver models. Reading the format and converting magnitudes to decibels are everyday operations for a board SI tool.

## The Touchstone format

A Touchstone file's extension names the port count: .s2p for 2 ports, .s4p for 4 (a differential pair has 4 single-ended ports). An option line such as "# GHz S MA R 50" gives the frequency unit, the parameter type (S), the number format (MA magnitude-angle, DB decibel-angle, or RI real-imaginary) and the reference impedance. Each frequency point then lists the frequency and the $N^2$ complex entries, so $2N^2 + 1$ real numbers. A 4-port file carries 16 S-parameters, 33 numbers, per frequency. The order is row-major except for one well-known quirk: 2-port files list $S_{11}, S_{21}, S_{12}, S_{22}$. Version 2.0 of the format adds keywords for mixed reference impedances and other metadata, which parsers must handle.

## Insertion loss in decibels

$S_{21}$ is the ratio of the voltage wave leaving port 2 to the wave entering port 1, with all ports terminated in the reference impedance. **Insertion loss** is $-20\log_{10}|S_{21}|$ in dB. Example: $|S_{21}| = 0.5$ is 6.02 dB of loss; 20 dB is $|S_{21}| = 0.1$. Board traces lose more at higher frequency, from conductor loss (skin effect, roughness) and dielectric loss (the laminate's loss tangent), so channel budgets are stated at the Nyquist frequency of the link, half the symbol rate. For matched sections the dB losses add, which is why loss is budgeted in dB per inch for each layer and material, and why a longer or lossier channel needs more equalization.

## Return loss and mismatch

$S_{11}$ is the wave reflected back into port 1. For a one-port load $Z_L$ measured with reference $Z_0$, $S_{11}$ equals the reflection coefficient $(Z_L - Z_0)/(Z_L + Z_0)$. **Return loss** is $-20\log_{10}|S_{11}|$; larger means a better match. Example: a 75 ohm load on a 50 ohm reference gives $|S_{11}| = 0.2$, a return loss of 13.98 dB; a 55 ohm load gives $|S_{11}| = 0.0476$, about 26.4 dB. Return loss of a channel reveals its discontinuities: vias, connector transitions and stubs show as peaks in $|S_{11}|$ and notches in $|S_{21}|$. Data quality matters too: a simulator needs passive and causal data, so tools check and enforce passivity and causality before using a Touchstone file in time-domain simulation.

## Going deeper

The Touchstone file format specification, published through the IBIS Open Forum. Pozar, "Microwave Engineering" (4th ed., 2011), chapter 4, on scattering parameters.

lesson:
# IBIS-AMI and SerDes channel simulation

Multi-gigabit serial links depend on equalization: transmit FFE, receive CTLE and DFE, and clock-data recovery. These are algorithms, often adaptive, that IBIS tables cannot describe. IBIS-AMI (Algorithmic Modeling Interface) extends IBIS with executable models that a channel simulator calls through a standard API. Combined with S-parameter channel models, they let a board designer predict eye opening and bit error rate before building the board.

## The AMI model structure

An IBIS-AMI model has two parts: the usual IBIS buffer for the analog front end, and an **algorithmic** part delivered as a compiled shared library plus an .ami parameter file that declares the model's settings (tap values, CTLE curves, adaptation modes). The simulator loads the library and calls three entry points: **AMI_Init**, which receives the channel's impulse response and may return an equalized one; **AMI_GetWave**, which processes blocks of waveform samples in the time domain; and **AMI_Close**, which frees the model's state. Because the interface is standard, any compliant simulator can run any vendor's model, and the vendor's equalization algorithms stay compiled and private. It is an engine seam in exactly the four-layer sense.

## Transmit FFE as a filter

A transmit feed-forward equalizer is a short FIR filter on the symbol stream: $y[n] = c_{-1} x[n+1] + c_0 x[n] + c_1 x[n-1]$, with a pre-cursor tap $c_{-1}$, a main tap $c_0$ and a post-cursor tap $c_1$, usually normalized so $|c_{-1}| + c_0 + |c_1| = 1$. Example with $c_{-1} = -0.1$, $c_0 = 0.7$, $c_1 = -0.2$: a transition, $x[n-1] = -1$, $x[n] = +1$, $x[n+1] = +1$, gives $-0.1 + 0.7 + 0.2 = 0.8$, while a repeated $+1$ after $+1$ gives $-0.1 + 0.7 - 0.2 = 0.4$. Transitions are emphasized relative to runs, a high-pass shaping that pre-compensates the channel's low-pass loss. Tap values are typical AMI parameters swept in channel simulation.

## Statistical and time-domain flows

A channel simulation cascades transmitter, Touchstone channel and receiver. In the **statistical** flow, if the equalization is linear and time-invariant, AMI_Init transforms the channel impulse response, and the simulator builds the eye and BER contours analytically from it, fast enough to sweep many settings. When the equalizer adapts or acts nonlinearly, as a **DFE** does by subtracting weighted past decisions to cancel post-cursor ISI, or as clock recovery does, the **time-domain** flow runs millions of bits through AMI_GetWave. Results can differ between simulators even with identical models, because jitter injection, sampling and BER extrapolation are each tool's own. A DFE cannot cancel pre-cursor ISI, since it only sees past bits; that is left to FFE and CTLE.

## Going deeper

The IBIS specification, chapters on the Algorithmic Modeling Interface. Hall and Heck, "Advanced Signal Integrity for High-Speed Digital Designs" (2009), chapter on equalization.
